reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A price fall in X raises the consumer's real purchasing power. Why can this reduce consumption of X?

options.label: A
options.text: An inferior good’s income effect can reduce its consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: The substitution effect always reduces consumption after a price fall.

options.label: C
options.text: A price fall rotates the budget line towards the origin.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal goods have lower consumption when real income rises.

explanation: A lower price raises real income. For an inferior good, higher real income reduces demand, so the income effect can offset some or all of the substitution toward X.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A price rise in X reduces real purchasing power. Why can this increase consumption of X?

options.label: A
options.text: An inferior good’s income effect can increase its consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: Substitution always favours the product that has become dearer.

options.label: C
options.text: A price rise shifts the budget line outward in parallel.

options.label: D
options.text: A price rise necessarily turns an inferior good into a normal good.

explanation: Lower real income raises demand for an inferior good. If this positive income effect is large enough, as for a Giffen good, it can outweigh substitution away from the now dearer X.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: For normal good X, why do the income and substitution effects of a fall in Px reinforce one another?

options.label: A
options.text: X becomes relatively dearer and real income falls.

options.label: B
options.text: The substitution effect vanishes because X is normal.

options.label: C
options.text: X becomes relatively cheaper and real income rises.

options.label: D
options.text: The budget line shifts inward in parallel.

explanation: The relative-price change encourages substitution toward X, and the gain in real purchasing power raises demand for X because it is normal.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Px falls. For normal good Y, the substitution effect caused by cheaper X reduces Y by 3 units, while the income effect raises Y by 5 units. What happens to Y overall?

options.label: A
options.text: Y decreases by 8 units.

options.label: B
options.text: Y decreases by 2 units.

options.label: C
options.text: Y increases by 2 units.

options.label: D
options.text: Y increases by 8 units.

explanation: The effects pull in opposite directions for Y: -3 + 5 = +2. This illustrates why the effect of another good's price change on Y can be ambiguous.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A consumer moves from E1 to E2 on the same indifference curve after a compensated fall in Px, then from E2 to E3 on a higher curve. What do the two movements represent?

options.label: A
options.text: E1→E2: substitution; E2→E3: income.

options.label: B
options.text: E1→E2: income; E2→E3: substitution.

options.label: C
options.text: E1→E2: income; E2→E3: income.

options.label: D
options.text: E1→E2: substitution; E2→E3: substitution.

explanation: The compensated movement keeps satisfaction at its original level while relative prices change, isolating substitution. The remaining movement reflects the change in real purchasing power.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: In a price-decomposition diagram, why must the compensated budget line be parallel to the new budget line?

options.label: A
options.text: Both must show the same money income.

options.label: B
options.text: Both must be tangent to the same indifference curve.

options.label: C
options.text: Both must reflect the same new relative prices.

options.label: D
options.text: Both must have the same intercepts.

explanation: Parallel budget lines have the same slope and therefore the same price ratio. The compensated line differs only in purchasing power so that the consumer can just reach the original satisfaction level.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An income increase shifts the budget line outward. The new optimum is on a higher indifference curve but contains less X. Which conclusion is justified?

options.label: A
options.text: The diagram establishes Giffen behaviour for X.

options.label: B
options.text: The diagram establishes inferiority, without establishing Giffen behaviour.

options.label: C
options.text: The diagram establishes normality because total satisfaction rises.

options.label: D
options.text: The diagram establishes no income response because relative prices stay fixed.

explanation: The fall in X as income rises identifies a negative income effect. Giffen classification additionally requires a particular response to X's own price, so it cannot be inferred from the income change alone.

prompt: A poor household consumes a staple X. When Px rises, the household cuts purchases of higher-quality foods and buys more X. Which mechanism could explain this?

options.label: A
options.text: Substitution towards X after its price rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Income outweighs substitution away from X.

options.label: C
options.text: A parallel outward shift in the budget line.

options.label: D
options.text: An income effect proving X normal.

explanation: If X is strongly inferior and takes a significant share of the budget, the loss of real income can force greater reliance on X. If this effect exceeds substitution away from X, Giffen behaviour results.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A consumer's tastes change after persuasive advertising at the same time that Px falls. What can be concluded from the original indifference map about the final quantity of X?

options.label: A
options.text: Price necessarily dominates tastes, so X increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Advertising changes money income, so X decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: Changed tastes prevent a definite original-map prediction.

options.label: D
options.text: Both changes necessarily offset, so X is unchanged.

explanation: The original map assumes preferences are held constant. A price change alters the constraint, while a taste change can shift the indifference map itself. Without more information the final choice is indeterminate.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A model draws smooth indifference curves between two goods, but one good can only be bought in whole units. What limitation does this highlight?

options.label: A
options.text: The budget line becomes vertical.

options.label: B
options.text: Substitution vanishes from every consumer choice.

options.label: C
options.text: The consumer ceases to face scarcity.

options.label: D
options.text: Smooth curves may misrepresent choices involving indivisible units.

explanation: Smooth curves treat quantities as continuously adjustable. With indivisible goods, small movements and exact tangencies may not be feasible, reducing the literal accuracy of the diagram.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Why is the use of only two goods a limitation of a simple indifference-curve diagram?

options.label: A
options.text: A two-good diagram simplifies a many-good allocation problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers cannot purchase more than two different goods.

options.label: C
options.text: A budget line cannot represent choices between two goods.

options.label: D
options.text: Two-good choices do not have a marginal substitution rate.

explanation: The two-good framework is useful for showing trade-offs clearly but abstracts from the much larger set of alternatives faced in real purchasing decisions.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Why can the tangency condition be an imperfect description of real consumer decisions?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers face no effective price or income constraints.

options.label: B
options.text: All consumers’ indifference curves have upward slopes.

options.label: C
options.text: Habits and defaults may replace continual re-optimisation.

options.label: D
options.text: Tangency requires the two goods to have identical prices.

explanation: The model assumes deliberate and consistent optimisation. Behavioural influences and decision costs can prevent consumers from locating or moving to the theoretical tangency point.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A researcher observes a consumer choosing bundle A over B today and B over A next week, with prices and income unchanged. What problem does this create for a fixed indifference map?

options.label: A
options.text: The consumer’s budget line must have changed.

options.label: B
options.text: The reversed choices establish indifference between the bundles, ruling out any possibility of changed preferences.

options.label: C
options.text: The consumer must have unlimited disposable income.

options.label: D
options.text: Preferences may have changed, undermining a fixed ranking.

explanation: A fixed indifference map represents a stable ordering of alternatives. Reversals with no budget change suggest context, information or preferences have changed.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement gives the most balanced evaluation of indifference-curve analysis?

options.label: A
options.text: Subjective preferences make the model entirely useless.

options.label: B
options.text: The model predicts each purchase exactly, even when tastes change and consumers cannot rank the available alternatives.

options.label: C
options.text: The model provides useful predictions under simplifying assumptions.

options.label: D
options.text: The model applies exclusively to consumers of Giffen goods.

explanation: The model clearly separates preferences from the budget constraint and can analyse income and substitution effects. Its usefulness is nevertheless limited by the assumptions needed to represent real behaviour with a stable, rational preference map.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.4 limitations of the model of indifference curves | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A consumer initially has 10 units of X at E1. After Px falls, the compensated point E2 contains 14 X and the final point E3 contains 12 X. How should the effects be described?

options.label: A
options.text: Substitution −4; income +2; price −2; normal.

options.label: B
options.text: Substitution +4; income −2; net +2; inferior.

options.label: C
options.text: Substitution +2; income +4; price +6; normal.

options.label: D
options.text: Substitution +4; income −6; price −2; Giffen.

explanation: E1→E2 raises X by 4, isolating substitution. E2→E3 reduces X by 2, so the income effect is negative. Final X is 2 above initial, so substitution dominates and X is inferior but non-Giffen.
reference: 7.2 Indifference curves and budget lines | 7.2.3 income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A fall in Px shifts the consumer from E1 to E3. E2 is the compensated point on the original indifference curve. Which comparison determines whether X is Giffen?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether E3 gives greater utility than E1.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the new budget has a flatter slope.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether income outweighs opposing substitution.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the price of Y has remained unchanged.

explanation: A price fall always creates a substitution movement toward X. Giffen behaviour requires the negative income movement away from X to be larger, leaving final X below its initial quantity.
